title: What is the most effective way to reduce ambiguity when prompting a Large Language Model?
feedback:
Reducing ambiguity is one of the primary goals of effective prompting. Explicit instructions and expected outputs help the model generate more reliable responses. Provide clear, specific instructions with context.
Source
answer1: Specify exactly what information is required and how it should be presented.
explanation1: Clear instructions and an explicit output expectation reduce uncertainty and improve response quality.
answer2: Use intentionally broad wording to encourage flexible interpretation.
explanation2: Broad wording increases the risk of inconsistent or irrelevant answers.
answer3: Rely on the model to infer any missing details.
explanation3: LLMs perform better when important information is explicitly provided.
answer4: Avoid describing the expected output format.
explanation4: Without an expected format, outputs are more likely to vary.

title: When is zero-shot prompting least reliable for generating Scrum-related outputs?
feedback:
Zero-shot prompting is most limited when the expected output depends on a specific pattern, template, or team convention that has not been provided. Zero-shot prompting relies on internal training knowledge and cannot infer team-specific formats.
Source
answer1: When the output must follow a format the model has not been shown.
explanation1: Without examples, the model may produce a plausible answer that does not match the required structure.
answer2: When the prompt includes a clear task description.
explanation2: A clear task description generally improves zero-shot prompting.
answer3: When the Scrum Team asks for a short response.
explanation3: Short responses can be generated with zero-shot prompts.
answer4: When the topic is familiar to the model.
explanation4: Familiar topics may still be handled reasonably well in zero-shot prompting.

title: An AI tool produces a code quality report for each Product Backlog item. What should the Scrum Team do before using it to support Done decisions?
feedback:
The question tests whether AI is treated as decision support rather than as the owner of quality. The Scrum Team may use AI-generated evidence, but the Increment is only Done when it satisfies the agreed quality measures. The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born.
Source
answer1: Validate how the report relates to the Definition of Done and keep human accountability for the decision.
explanation1: AI reports may support inspection, but the Scrum Team must decide whether the Increment meets the Definition of Done.
answer2: Use the AI report as the only evidence that the item is Done.
explanation2: One automated report is not enough unless it satisfies all quality measures in the Definition of Done.
answer3: Let the Product Owner override the Definition of Done when the report looks positive.
explanation3: The Product Owner cannot redefine Done item by item based on AI output.
answer4: Ask the AI to rewrite the Definition of Done after each Sprint.
explanation4: The Definition of Done should be inspected and adapted by people, not delegated entirely to AI.

title: Which option describes the broadest responsible AI concern for a Scrum Team adopting AI tools?
feedback:
The question evaluates whether responsible AI is understood as a multidimensional concern. A Scrum Team should not reduce AI ethics to convenience, speed, or tone. Using AI responsibly and ethically is mandatory to prevent harm, ensure fairness, and maintain public trust.
Source
answer1: The team must consider bias, data protection, transparency, and human accountability.
explanation1: This answer covers several major ethical dimensions rather than focusing on only one issue.
answer2: The team must mainly ensure the AI tool is fast enough for daily work.
explanation2: Speed can be useful, but it is not the broadest responsible AI concern.
answer3: The team must focus only on whether the AI output sounds professional.
explanation3: A professional tone does not make AI output ethical, safe, or reliable.
answer4: The team must ensure AI is used in every Scrum event to maximize adoption.
explanation4: Broad adoption does not address ethical use or risk management.

title: A Scrum Master wants to use AI before a difficult stakeholder alignment session. What is the best use of AI?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether AI is used to strengthen preparation rather than control the group. A Scrum Master may use AI to explore facilitation approaches, but the session must remain human-led and inclusive. I'm facilitating a cross-cultural session—what icebreakers promote psychological safety?
Source
answer1: Ask AI for agenda ideas, facilitation techniques, and risks to consider before the session.
explanation1: This keeps AI in a supporting role while the Scrum Master remains responsible for facilitation.
answer2: Ask AI to predict which stakeholder is most likely to resist and isolate them.
explanation2: This may create bias and damage trust before the workshop even begins.
answer3: Ask AI to replace the facilitator so the discussion appears neutral.
explanation3: AI cannot take accountability for facilitation quality or group dynamics.
answer4: Ask AI to generate the final alignment statement without stakeholder input.
explanation4: Alignment requires real participation, not a pre-written conclusion.

title: An AI dashboard publicly compares each Developer's output and the team becomes less open during the Daily Scrum. What is the best response?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the Scrum Master can identify that AI-supported measurement may damage openness and psychological safety. The responsible action is to inspect the practice with the team rather than normalize surveillance. Keeping psychological safety high is a must.
Source
answer1: Raise the issue with the Scrum Team and inspect whether the dashboard harms transparency, safety, and collaboration.
explanation1: The Scrum Master should help the team examine whether the AI dashboard supports or damages effective Scrum.
answer2: Ask quieter Developers to speak more so the dashboard appears less harmful.
explanation2: This treats the symptom rather than addressing the tool's effect on psychological safety.
answer3: Continue using the dashboard because public metrics increase accountability.
explanation3: Public individual metrics may create fear and reduce openness rather than improve accountability.
answer4: Ask the AI vendor to hide the lowest scores without changing the practice.
explanation4: Hiding some data does not resolve the underlying trust and collaboration issue.

title: Which capability would most clearly distinguish AGI from today's narrow AI systems?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands that AGI is about general intellectual capability, not simply fluency, speed, or scale. Current AI may be useful, but it is not equivalent to broad human-level intelligence. potential form of AI
Source
answer1: The ability to transfer learning and reasoning across many unrelated intellectual domains.
explanation1: AGI would require broad generalization beyond a single task, tool, or domain-specific capability.
answer2: The ability to generate fluent text in response to a prompt.
explanation2: Fluent text generation can be produced by narrow generative AI and does not prove AGI.
answer3: The ability to classify data faster than a human specialist.
explanation3: Speed and classification accuracy can exist in narrow AI systems.
answer4: The ability to use a larger context window than previous models.
explanation4: A larger context window improves capacity, but it does not establish general intelligence.

title: A Scrum Master wants team members to reuse prompts for different facilitation situations. What is the best approach?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the Scrum Master can make prompting a shared team capability. A reusable prompt library improves consistency because team members can access, adapt, and improve common templates. Prompt Library for Facilitators
Source
answer1: Create a shared prompt library with categorized templates and editable variables.
explanation1: A categorized library makes prompts easier to find, reuse, and adapt across facilitation contexts.
answer2: Ask everyone to save prompts privately in their own notes.
explanation2: Private storage prevents shared learning and reduces consistency.
answer3: Use only one universal prompt for all facilitation needs.
explanation3: One prompt is unlikely to fit different facilitation goals, contexts, and team dynamics.
answer4: Ask the AI to remember the team's preferred prompts without documenting them.
explanation4: Relying on model memory is unreliable and weakens transparency for the team.

title: A Scrum Team proposes feeding stakeholder interview transcripts into an AI assistant. What should be done first?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the learner can apply responsible AI principles before using stakeholder data. AI may support analysis, but personal or sensitive information should not be processed without purpose, consent, and minimization. Responsible & Ethical AI
Source
answer1: Clarify the intended use, remove unnecessary sensitive information, and confirm consent before processing.
explanation1: The team should protect stakeholder information and ensure AI use is transparent, limited, and justified.
answer2: Upload the transcripts first and review privacy issues only if the AI produces useful insights.
explanation2: Privacy and consent should be addressed before processing the data, not after value is proven.
answer3: Ask the AI assistant to identify which parts of the transcripts are sensitive after upload.
explanation3: Sensitive information should be minimized before the data is shared with the tool.
answer4: Keep the transcripts in the tool permanently to improve future responses.
explanation4: Permanent storage increases risk and may exceed the original purpose of collection.

title: A manager wants an AI system to automatically distribute Sprint work to Developers according to their skill profiles. What should the Scrum Master challenge first?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the Scrum Master can distinguish helpful AI support from harmful delegation of team accountability. Automatic assignment may reduce collaboration and turn the Sprint Backlog into a management-controlled work queue. The A3 Framework: Assist, Automate, Avoid - A Decision System for AI Delegation
Source
answer1: Whether the system removes the Developers' ability to self-manage the Sprint Backlog.
explanation1: The Scrum Master should challenge practices that replace team decision-making with automated assignment.
answer2: Whether the AI system can connect to the organization's workflow tool.
explanation2: Integration is an implementation concern, not the main Scrum risk.
answer3: Whether the AI system can create more detailed work descriptions.
explanation3: More detail does not solve the risk of replacing self-management.
answer4: Whether the AI system can estimate individual capacity accurately.
explanation4: Individual capacity estimates may reinforce assignment control rather than team ownership.

title: A Scrum Master wants AI support for assessing delivery risks in a complex Sprint. Which prompting technique is most suitable?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether Chain-of-Thought is understood as useful for complex reasoning. Risk analysis benefits from structured reasoning because the Scrum Team needs to inspect assumptions before acting. Encouraging the model to break down its reasoning
Source
answer1: Instruct the model to analyze the situation step by step before recommending actions.
explanation1: Step-by-step prompting helps structure the analysis and makes the recommendation easier to inspect.
answer2: Ask for the shortest possible answer to avoid overthinking the risk.
explanation2: A very short answer may miss important dependencies or assumptions.
answer3: Ask the model to respond with maximum creativity and no constraints.
explanation3: Risk assessment requires disciplined reasoning, not unconstrained creativity.
answer4: Use a role-based prompt and assume the model's judgment becomes authoritative.
explanation4: A role prompt may help perspective, but the Scrum Team still needs to inspect the output.

title: A suspected deepfake audio message from an executive asks teams to change priorities immediately. What should the Scrum Master do?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether learners understand that deepfake risks require verification before action. AI-generated or manipulated media can create false urgency, so the Scrum Master should support calm inspection and transparent communication. Using AI responsibly and ethically is mandatory to prevent harm, ensure fairness, and maintain public trust.
Source
answer1: Pause action on the message, verify it through official channels, and help communicate the verified information.
explanation1: This protects the team from acting on manipulated media and supports responsible decision-making.
answer2: Follow the message because it appears to come from a senior leader.
explanation2: Apparent authority is not enough when the message may be synthetic or manipulated.
answer3: Ask the AI tool that created the transcript to decide whether the audio is authentic.
explanation3: AI detection may assist, but authenticity should be verified through trusted organizational channels.
answer4: Tell the team to ignore all future executive audio messages.
explanation4: A broad rejection of all audio communication is excessive and does not solve the specific risk.

title: Developers want to use AI to propose acceptance criteria during refinement. What should the Scrum Master encourage?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether AI is introduced as an inspectable learning experiment rather than a large process change. Product Backlog refinement should remain collaborative, with AI used as support rather than replacement. The A3 Framework: Assist, Automate, Avoid - A Decision System for AI Delegation
Source
answer1: Try it on a limited set of Product Backlog items and compare usefulness, quality, and team understanding.
explanation1: A small experiment allows the team to inspect whether AI improves refinement without overcommitting.
answer2: Apply it to the entire Product Backlog immediately to maximize learning speed.
explanation2: Using AI broadly before inspection can create rework, dependency, and hidden quality issues.
answer3: Use only delivery speed as the success measure.
explanation3: Delivery speed alone ignores whether the items become clearer, more valuable, or better understood.
answer4: Allow AI-generated acceptance criteria to bypass team discussion.
explanation4: Skipping discussion weakens shared understanding and collaboration during refinement.

title: How does AI affect the Scrum Master's role in a Scrum Team?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether AI is seen as an aid rather than a replacement. The Scrum Master role may evolve as tools change, but the accountability for helping the team and organization remains human. Is AI Taking My Job?
Source
answer1: It may change how some activities are performed, while human accountability remains with the Scrum Master.
explanation1: The best answer recognizes both evolution and continuity: AI can assist work, but accountability does not move to AI.
answer2: It makes the role identical to before because AI should not influence Scrum Master activities.
explanation2: This ignores that AI can assist preparation, analysis, facilitation design, and learning.
answer3: It replaces the Scrum Master whenever the team uses AI for retrospectives.
explanation3: Using AI in retrospectives does not replace human facilitation and coaching accountability.
answer4: It transfers accountability for impediment removal to AI agents.
explanation4: AI can help surface patterns, but it cannot own accountability for helping remove impediments.

title: A Scrum Team asks AI to improve its Definition of Done. The output contains useful quality checks and unrelated process rules. What is the best response?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the Scrum Team can filter AI-generated content responsibly. The key is not whether AI produced the suggestion, but whether the item strengthens the shared quality standard for the Increment. The Definition of Done creates transparency by providing everyone a shared understanding of what work was completed as part of the Increment.
Source
answer1: Discuss the output as a team and separate valuable quality measures from unrelated suggestions.
explanation1: The team should treat AI output as input for inspection, not as an automatically valid update.
answer2: Add every item to avoid missing any possible quality concern.
explanation2: Adding irrelevant items can make the Definition of Done confusing and harder to use.
answer3: Remove every AI-generated item because the Definition of Done must be written manually.
explanation3: Rejecting all AI assistance ignores potentially useful suggestions that the team can inspect.
answer4: Let the Product Owner alone decide which AI-generated items are kept.
explanation4: The Definition of Done should support the whole Scrum Team's shared understanding of quality.

title: A stakeholder says the team should accept AI recommendations whenever the model reports high confidence. What is the best response?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether learners can avoid over-reliance on AI confidence. AI output may be useful, but responsible use requires human validation and accountability before decisions are made. The A3 Framework: Assist, Automate, Avoid - A Decision System for AI Delegation
Source
answer1: Treat confidence as one signal and validate the recommendation through human judgment and context.
explanation1: A confidence score can support inspection, but it does not remove the need for accountability, explainability, and review.
answer2: Accept the recommendation because confidence scores reduce human bias.
explanation2: AI confidence can be misleading and does not guarantee fairness or correctness.
answer3: Reject every AI recommendation that includes a confidence score.
explanation3: A confidence score is not the problem; blind reliance on it is.
answer4: Let the Product Owner follow the AI privately and inform the team afterward.
explanation4: Private reliance on AI reduces transparency and weakens shared accountability.

title: An AI assistant answers compliance questions confidently, but users cannot see where the information came from. What should be improved first?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether responsible AI is understood as more than generating confident answers. Compliance-related outputs need transparency, source grounding, and human validation when the impact is significant. Using AI responsibly and ethically is mandatory to prevent harm, ensure fairness, and maintain public trust.
Source
answer1: Provide traceable sources, uncertainty handling, and human review for sensitive compliance topics.
explanation1: Compliance advice can create risk, so users need source transparency and escalation for high-impact cases.
answer2: Make the chatbot sound more formal to increase user confidence.
explanation2: A formal tone does not make unsupported compliance advice reliable.
answer3: Allow the chatbot to answer without disclaimers to keep the experience simple.
explanation3: Removing disclaimers may mislead users about the limits of the advice.
answer4: Train users to accept the chatbot as the single compliance authority.
explanation4: High-risk compliance decisions should not depend solely on AI output.

title: Which behavior most clearly separates agentic AI from a standard AI assistant?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the learner understands that agentic AI is not simply any AI output. The key distinction is an autonomous, multi-step process aimed at achieving a goal. AI systems can break down complex problems, plan, use tools, and act in a loop
Source
answer1: It can plan multiple steps, select tools, and continue acting toward a defined objective.
explanation1: Agentic AI is goal-oriented and can coordinate steps rather than only answering one request.
answer2: It can generate a fluent answer to a question.
explanation2: Fluent generation is common in LLMs but does not prove agentic behavior.
answer3: It can summarize a document when a user uploads it.
explanation3: Summarization is a task response, not necessarily autonomous goal pursuit.
answer4: It can classify a defect report into a predefined category.
explanation4: Classification is bounded and does not show planning or iterative action.

title: Which option is the clearest example of ANI in a Scrum Team's work environment?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the learner can recognize ANI in a practical Scrum context. Ticket classification is a narrow, task-specific AI capability, even if it provides useful support to the team. Artificial Narrow Intelligence (ANI)
Source
answer1: An AI tool that classifies incoming support tickets by topic.
explanation1: This is ANI because the tool performs a specific classification task within a limited domain.
answer2: An AI system that understands and solves any organizational problem independently.
explanation2: This describes broad general capability, not Artificial Narrow Intelligence.
answer3: An AI agent that replaces all Scrum roles and adapts to any business context.
explanation3: This suggests generalized autonomous capability, not a narrow AI use case.
answer4: A system that develops consciousness after learning from team conversations.
explanation4: Consciousness is not part of ANI and is not a realistic description of current narrow AI.

title: What is the most accurate statement about Chain-of-Thought prompting?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether Chain-of-Thought is understood as a prompting aid rather than a guarantee mechanism. A structured answer can still be wrong, incomplete, or unsupported. Chain-of-Thought (CoT)
Source
answer1: It can help organize reasoning, but it does not make AI responses automatically reliable.
explanation1: The technique may improve how a model approaches complex analysis, but the result still needs review.
answer2: It guarantees factual accuracy by forcing the model to reason logically.
explanation2: Logical-looking reasoning can still contain incorrect assumptions or false information.
answer3: It prevents hallucinations by exposing every step of the answer.
explanation3: Chain-of-Thought may reduce ambiguity, but it does not eliminate hallucinations.
answer4: It replaces the need for subject-matter expertise in complex decisions.
explanation4: Subject-matter expertise remains necessary to validate AI-generated conclusions.

title: A Scrum Team is stuck repeating the same improvement ideas during a retrospective. What is the best AI-supported action?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether AI is used to enrich retrospective thinking without removing team ownership. AI may suggest perspectives and themes, but the Scrum Team should inspect and adapt the ideas themselves. brainstorm ideas, outline strategy, facilitate collaboration
Source
answer1: Ask AI to propose different viewpoints and organize the team's existing ideas into themes.
explanation1: This helps the team break out of repetitive thinking while preserving human inspection and discussion.
answer2: Let AI decide which improvement action the team must take next Sprint.
explanation2: The team should decide its improvement action, not delegate it to AI.
answer3: Use AI to replace the retrospective discussion with an automated report.
explanation3: A report cannot replace the team's shared inspection and adaptation.
answer4: Ask AI to ignore previous ideas and invent a completely unrelated improvement plan.
explanation4: Ignoring team context can produce irrelevant or low-value suggestions.

title: Developers repeatedly mention deployment delays, but the team cannot see a clear root cause. What is the best AI-supported approach?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether AI is used to strengthen Retrospective preparation rather than automate conclusions. Reviewing past notes can reveal patterns, but the Scrum Team still needs to inspect meaning and choose adaptations. AI-Enhanced Sprint Retrospective
Source
answer1: Analyze past Retrospective notes to identify repeated themes and bring them to the team for discussion.
explanation1: This helps the team inspect evidence across Sprints while keeping interpretation and action selection human-led.
answer2: Ask AI to rank Developers according to how often their work caused deployment delays.
explanation2: Individual ranking can create blame and does not support collaborative problem solving.
answer3: Let AI decide which process change the team must implement immediately.
explanation3: AI recommendations should be inspected by the team rather than treated as mandatory decisions.
answer4: Ignore historical notes because the Retrospective should focus only on the latest Sprint.
explanation4: Historical patterns may reveal recurring impediments that a single Sprint view can miss.

title: An AI assistant summarizes survey responses and suggests three Retrospective topics. How should the Scrum Master introduce them?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the Scrum Master introduces AI assistance transparently and collaboratively. The AI summary should create a better starting point, not replace the team's inspection and adaptation. A practical way to leverage AI to increase the Sprint Retrospective effectiveness.
Source
answer1: Offer them as optional prompts for the team to inspect and adapt during the Retrospective.
explanation1: This keeps the Retrospective collaborative and avoids treating AI analysis as the final interpretation.
answer2: Use them as the confirmed agenda to save time.
explanation2: Saving time does not justify removing team participation in shaping the discussion.
answer3: Hide that AI was used so participants are not biased.
explanation3: Lack of transparency may reduce trust if participants later discover AI involvement.
answer4: Ask AI to select which topic the team must act on first.
explanation4: AI may suggest themes, but the Scrum Team should choose what matters most.

title: A Product Owner receives an AI-generated competitor summary that sounds credible but includes unfamiliar statistics. What is the best next step?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the learner can distinguish credibility of style from credibility of evidence. AI-generated product research should be checked against authoritative sources before it is used or shared. Using AI responsibly and ethically is mandatory to prevent harm, ensure fairness, and maintain public trust.
Source
answer1: Check the statistics against authoritative sources before sharing the summary.
explanation1: Unknown statistics should be validated before they are used in stakeholder communication or product decisions.
answer2: Share the summary if the AI response includes confident wording.
explanation2: Confidence in wording does not make the statistics accurate.
answer3: Ask the AI to rewrite the summary in a more cautious tone.
explanation3: A cautious tone may reduce overconfidence but does not validate the data.
answer4: Compare three AI-generated summaries and keep the most detailed one.
explanation4: Detail does not guarantee accuracy, and multiple AI outputs may repeat the same error.

title: What is the primary purpose of backpropagation during AI model training?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the learner understands backpropagation as part of how neural networks learn. The technique connects prediction error to weight adjustment so the model can improve through training. Backpropagation
Source
answer1: To calculate how errors should change the model's weights.
explanation1: Backpropagation helps the training process determine how each weight should be adjusted to reduce future error.
answer2: To permanently store user conversations for later retrieval.
explanation2: Conversation storage is unrelated to backpropagation and raises separate privacy concerns.
answer3: To convert unstructured text into a shorter compressed file.
explanation3: Text compression is not the purpose of backpropagation.
answer4: To manually define rules that replace machine learning.
explanation4: Backpropagation is part of machine learning; it does not replace learning with manual rules.

title: Why should a Scrum Team try a low-risk AI experiment during a Sprint and discuss it in the Retrospective?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether AI adoption is treated as an empirical process. The goal is not adoption for its own sake, but learning whether a specific AI use improves the Scrum Team's effectiveness. The A3 Framework: Assist, Automate, Avoid - A Decision System for AI Delegation
Source
answer1: To learn from actual use and decide whether the AI practice improves the team's work.
explanation1: The team gains evidence from real experience and can adapt its use of AI based on observed impact.
answer2: To force AI adoption before the team becomes resistant.
explanation2: Forcing adoption reduces ownership and does not prove the practice is valuable.
answer3: To let the Scrum Master control how Developers use AI.
explanation3: The Scrum Master should support learning, not control Developer practices.
answer4: To replace the Retrospective with an AI-generated improvement report.
explanation4: An AI report cannot replace the team's inspection and adaptation.

title: A Product Backlog item has acceptance criteria that are too broad to guide development. What should the Scrum Team do with AI assistance?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the Scrum Team can use AI to improve refinement without delegating product judgment. Clearer criteria are useful only when validated against the goal, user need, and team understanding. Product Backlog items that can be Done by the Scrum Team within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in a Sprint Planning event.
Source
answer1: Ask AI to propose more specific criteria, then review them against the Product Goal and stakeholder need.
explanation1: This keeps AI in an assisting role while the Scrum Team validates value, clarity, and fit.
answer2: Ask AI to split the item and approve all generated criteria automatically.
explanation2: AI-generated splits and criteria still require human review and shared understanding.
answer3: Ask AI to replace the Product Owner's responsibility for clarifying the item.
explanation3: AI cannot take over product accountability or stakeholder understanding.
answer4: Ignore the criteria until the Sprint Review reveals whether the item meets expectations.
explanation4: Waiting until the Sprint Review increases the risk of misalignment and waste.

title: During refinement preparation, the Product Owner has many stakeholder comments from different sources. What is the best AI-supported action?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether AI is used as a sense-making tool for refinement preparation. Grouping stakeholder feedback can help the Scrum Team inspect possible needs, but it should not become automated decision-making. The Scrum Team may refine these items during this process, which increases understanding and confidence.
Source
answer1: Use AI to cluster related feedback and highlight themes for the Scrum Team to review.
explanation1: Clustering helps the Product Owner prepare refinement while preserving human judgment and team discussion.
answer2: Ask AI to convert all comments directly into Sprint Backlog tasks.
explanation2: Sprint Backlog work emerges during Sprint Planning and should not be created automatically from comments.
answer3: Let AI decide which stakeholders should be ignored because their feedback is inconsistent.
explanation3: AI should not exclude stakeholder input without accountable human review.
answer4: Use AI to estimate all items so refinement can focus only on delivery dates.
explanation4: Estimation should involve the Developers and should not replace refinement conversations.

title: A Scrum Team has a preferred Sprint Goal format and wants AI to follow it consistently. What should the prompt include?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the learner can select the right prompt technique for format matching. Few-shot prompting is useful when the model needs to imitate a known structure rather than invent a new one. Few-Shot Prompting
Source
answer1: Two or three examples of Sprint Goals that already match the team's preferred format.
explanation1: Few-shot examples give the AI a concrete pattern to imitate and improve format consistency.
answer2: A request to be creative and invent a stronger Sprint Goal format.
explanation2: Creativity may produce useful ideas, but it can also move away from the team's agreed structure.
answer3: Only the Sprint Backlog items selected for the Sprint.
explanation3: Sprint Backlog items provide context, but they do not show the expected Sprint Goal format.
answer4: A role prompt telling the AI to act as an expert Scrum Master.
explanation4: A role prompt can shape perspective, but examples are stronger for reproducing a specific format.

title: Why is RAG useful when an organization needs AI answers based on current internal policies?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the learner understands RAG as a grounding mechanism. For internal policies, RAG can retrieve relevant approved content and use it to support the response without retraining the LLM. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
Source
answer1: It can retrieve relevant policy content and use it as context for the generated answer.
explanation1: RAG is useful because it grounds the model's response in selected documents rather than relying only on pre-trained knowledge.
answer2: It permanently stores every policy inside the model's weights.
explanation2: RAG retrieves content at use time; it does not necessarily change model weights.
answer3: It removes the need to validate whether the retrieved policy is correct.
explanation3: Retrieved information still needs governance, maintenance, and validation.
answer4: It allows the AI to answer without any source documents.
explanation4: RAG specifically relies on source documents or knowledge repositories.

title: AI-generated Sprint Review summaries vary in headings, order, and level of detail. Which prompting practice is most effective?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the learner can correct inconsistent AI output through prompt design. Few-shot examples demonstrate the target structure and help the model produce reports that are easier to reuse. Few-Shot Prompting
Source
answer1: Provide examples that show the exact headings, sequence, and detail level expected.
explanation1: Few-shot examples make the desired format concrete and reduce output variation.
answer2: Ask the AI to be more professional in every response.
explanation2: Professional tone does not guarantee a consistent structure.
answer3: Manually reformat every response after generation.
explanation3: Manual formatting treats the symptom instead of improving the prompt.
answer4: Remove all formatting constraints so the AI can choose the best structure.
explanation4: Removing constraints usually increases format variability.

title: A Scrum Team starts accepting AI-generated architecture choices without team discussion. What should the Scrum Master raise?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether AI is used as decision support rather than as a replacement for team reasoning. The Scrum Master should help the team preserve collaboration, ownership, and accountability for technical decisions. The A3 Framework: Assist, Automate, Avoid - A Decision System for AI Delegation
Source
answer1: The team may be outsourcing technical accountability instead of inspecting options together.
explanation1: AI can inform architecture discussions, but the Scrum Team should still own the decision and its consequences.
answer2: The AI may generate architecture diagrams in an inconsistent format.
explanation2: Formatting is not the central risk when technical judgment is being delegated.
answer3: The Product Owner should approve all architecture decisions before implementation.
explanation3: Architecture decisions require Developer collaboration and cannot simply be transferred to the Product Owner.
answer4: The team should ban AI from all technical discussions.
explanation4: The issue is not AI use itself, but blind delegation of judgment to AI.

title: The Scrum Team asks AI to analyze several past Retrospective notes and suggest improvement actions. What is the best approach?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the learner can select RAG when the quality of the answer depends on specific source material. Retrospective recommendations should be based on the team's real evidence, not only on general Scrum knowledge. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
Source
answer1: Use RAG so the AI can retrieve and use the team's actual notes before generating recommendations.
explanation1: This allows the recommendations to be grounded in the team's real historical data rather than broad Scrum guidance.
answer2: Ask the AI to act as an expert Scrum Master without providing the notes.
explanation2: A role prompt may shape perspective, but it cannot ground recommendations in unavailable team notes.
answer3: Provide examples of well-written action items from other teams.
explanation3: Examples may improve output style, but they do not supply the team's actual data.
answer4: Ask the AI to produce the most common retrospective improvements used in Scrum.
explanation4: Common improvements may be generic and may not address the team's real patterns.

title: Employees need accurate answers from current company procedures stored across many repositories. What AI approach best supports this?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the learner can select RAG when answers must be grounded in current internal sources. The system should retrieve approved content rather than depend on generic model memory. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
Source
answer1: Index the approved documents and use RAG to retrieve relevant content for each answer.
explanation1: This makes the response more traceable and connected to approved company information.
answer2: Ask the LLM to infer procedures from general industry knowledge.
explanation2: General knowledge may be outdated or inconsistent with the organization's real procedures.
answer3: Compress all documents into a short manual and prompt the model with it once.
explanation3: A short manual may omit important details and quickly become outdated.
answer4: Allow the AI to answer from memory and flag uncertainty only when users complain.
explanation4: Waiting for complaints does not ensure reliability or source transparency.

title: A Scrum Master coaches a team that is nervous about using AI. What is the best way to build confidence?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the Scrum Master supports AI adoption through safe, shared learning. The best approach is to connect AI use to a real need, keep the experiment small, and inspect the outcome with the team. Assist (AI drafts, you actively review and decide)
Source
answer1: Start with a small AI experiment that supports a specific team problem and review the results together.
explanation1: A focused experiment lowers risk and helps the team learn from real experience instead of abstract training alone.
answer2: Mandate daily AI usage so the team becomes comfortable quickly.
explanation2: Mandatory usage can create anxiety and does not guarantee meaningful learning.
answer3: Avoid AI until the team requests it without any encouragement.
explanation3: Complete avoidance may miss opportunities to learn safely and responsibly.
answer4: Ask the most technical Developer to use AI privately and report back later.
explanation4: Private learning limits shared understanding and does not build team confidence together.

title: A Product Owner wants AI support for a proposal that must reflect customers, compliance, operations, and Developers. What should the prompt request?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the learner understands how to use AI to explore stakeholder diversity. Explicitly asking for multiple perspectives and trade-offs helps the Scrum Team inspect the proposal more thoroughly. Generate multiple distinct possibilities
Source
answer1: Ask for the proposal to be reviewed from each perspective, including tensions and trade-offs.
explanation1: This makes the output richer by surfacing how different stakeholders may view the same proposal differently.
answer2: Ask AI to write from the Product Owner perspective only.
explanation2: A single Product Owner perspective may miss concerns from other stakeholders.
answer3: Ask AI to produce the most persuasive version of the proposal.
explanation3: A persuasive proposal may hide trade-offs or stakeholder concerns.
answer4: Ask AI to summarize the proposal without adding perspectives.
explanation4: A summary may clarify content, but it does not ensure broad stakeholder representation.

title: Developers use AI to draft user stories, but each output follows a different structure. What is the best improvement?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether the Scrum Master can address inconsistent AI-assisted user story drafting through a team-level prompt standard. Reusable templates make the expected structure visible and easier to inspect. Prompt Library for Facilitators
Source
answer1: Create a reusable prompt template that specifies the desired user story structure and quality criteria.
explanation1: The template reduces variability by making the expected output explicit for everyone using AI.
answer2: Ask the AI to decide the best structure each time.
explanation2: Letting AI choose the structure increases inconsistency and may reduce shared understanding.
answer3: Ban individual prompting and appoint a single prompt owner.
explanation3: This prevents the team from building shared prompting skills.
answer4: Use longer prompts without agreeing on a common format.
explanation4: Longer prompts do not guarantee consistent structure if the expected format is unclear.

title: An AI assistant proposes escalating an impediment in a way that may bypass the organization's governance process. What is the best next step?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether learners understand that AI recommendations can sound reasonable while still violating governance. The Scrum Master should verify the specific action before using it in an impediment plan. Assist (AI drafts, you actively review and decide)
Source
answer1: Check the proposed escalation path against current governance rules before acting.
explanation1: The Scrum Master should verify whether the AI recommendation fits the organization's actual policies and constraints.
answer2: Accept the escalation path because AI considered multiple options.
explanation2: Considering multiple options does not prove that the selected option is compliant.
answer3: Ask the AI to rewrite the recommendation in a more policy-friendly tone.
explanation3: Changing the tone does not validate compliance with governance rules.
answer4: Remove all AI-generated escalation suggestions from future prompts.
explanation4: The issue is not escalation suggestions in general, but unvalidated recommendations that may conflict with policy.

title: Developers stop reading Product Backlog items because AI summaries are provided before each refinement session. What is the best response?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether AI summaries are treated as support rather than a substitute for team learning. If Developers disengage from the Product Backlog, the Scrum Master should help the team adapt the practice. The Scrum Team may refine these items during this process, which increases understanding and confidence.
Source
answer1: Discuss whether the summaries are reducing shared understanding and change how they are used.
explanation1: The team should inspect whether the AI support is replacing the engagement needed for effective refinement.
answer2: Make the summaries longer so Developers receive more information.
explanation2: Longer summaries may increase dependency on AI rather than restore active engagement.
answer3: Ask the AI to mark which Developers need to read each item.
explanation3: This turns engagement into assignment and may reduce shared ownership.
answer4: Let the Product Owner handle all backlog understanding before Sprint Planning.
explanation4: Developers need to understand the work they may select and deliver; this cannot be fully delegated to the Product Owner.

title: An AI system recommends revising a customer refund rule to reduce operational costs. No stakeholders have reviewed the impact. What should happen next?
feedback:
This question evaluates whether AI is treated as decision support rather than an autonomous policy authority. Customer-facing policy changes can affect trust and fairness, so human review and stakeholder input are required before implementation. Avoid (AI stays out; humans decide and act)
Source
answer1: Use the recommendation as input and submit it to formal human review with stakeholder consultation.
explanation1: The AI recommendation may be useful, but policy changes need people to inspect value, risk, fairness, and impact before action.
answer2: Implement the change immediately because it improves efficiency.
explanation2: Efficiency alone does not justify changing a customer-facing policy without review.
answer3: Ask the AI to notify stakeholders after deployment.
explanation3: Stakeholders should be involved before implementation, not only informed afterward.
answer4: Hide the AI contribution to avoid unnecessary debate.
explanation4: Hiding AI involvement weakens transparency and trust.
